To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the in-situ μRaman spectroscopy is a powerful tool to study the stress in TSV structures.

the in-situ μRaman spectroscopy is used to measure stresses of TSVs and the axial stress exhibits a linear relationship with Cu protrusion height, which can be used to estimate the Cu protrusion behavior during thermal cycling.

the in-situ μ-raman spectroscopy characterization at different temperatures is capable of revealing the stress evolution in Si near Cu interconnects and the axial stress exhibited linear relationship with the protrusion behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stress distribution in TSVs during thermal cycling, and the relationship between Cu interconnect protrusion and the Si stress is revealed for the first time.
the evolution of the stress in Si and its relationship with the protrusion behavior of the Cu filled TSV.
the evolution of the stresses during annealing and their relationship with Cu protrusion behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thermal stress evolution during annealing step is a key factor to the Cu protrusions in TSV structures.
the Cu protrusion behavior in the TSVs was mainly induced by the thermal stress evolution in the Si.
the compressive stress in Si near the Cu TSV is responsible for the Cu protrusion behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the compressive stress induced by thermal cycling during annealing can cause Cu protrusion in the Cu filled TSV structure.
the Cu protrusion is mainly induced by the thermal stresses in Si during thermal cycling.
the Cu protrusion behavior was mainly determined by the thermal stresses in Si during the thermal cycling process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Cu protrusion behavior can be predicted by the Si stress evolution in TSV structures.
the protrusion height is proportional to the axial stress of Si near the Cu filled TSV.

μ-RS can be used as a nondestructive technique to characterize the thermal stresses in TSVs, and to provide a better understanding of the relationship between the stress in Si and Cu protrusion behavior.
